decisions.latin: psalmum dícite nómini ejus … psallat tibi: psalmum dicat nómini tuo
decisions.why: *Psalmum dícere* is *entoar um salmo* in the finished psalms (17:50, 26:6b, 56:8, 60:9), of D25's family, and *psállere* is *entoar salmos* (D25). In 65:4 the two stand side by side (*psallat tibi: psalmum dicat*); the Greek has one verb twice (ψαλάτωσαν), and the Portuguese keeps the Latin's near-repetition: *entoe salmos … entoe um salmo*. *Cantar* cannot stand, because *cantáre* is its verb (D25). Each colon of 65:4 reads alone as the Epiphany versicle *Omnis terra adóret te, et psallat tibi* (grep: Sancti/01-06 and the Matins antiphon).

options.label: entoai um salmo / entoe salmos / entoe um salmo
cantai um salmo / cante salmos / cante um salmo
entoai um salmo / cante / entoe um salmo
options.note: avoids the near-repetition in 65:4 at the cost of the glossary verb for psállere

decisions.why: The Latin gives glory *to his praise* (δότε δόξαν αἰνέσει αὐτοῦ; DRB 'give glory to his praise'). It is a strange phrase and the Latin's own; the Hebrew 'make his praise glorious' is another reading. MS1932 turns it into *tributai-lhe gloriosos louvores*, which explains and drops the dative. *dai* is safe at the vós imperative (past *dei*).

options.label: tornai glorioso o seu louvor
options.note: the Hebrew's sense; not the Latin's build

options.label: rendei glória ao seu louvor
options.note: a devotional verb for *dare*; *render* is not in the glossary

decisions.why: The *multitúdo* row is *multidão* (*na multidão da vossa misericórdia*), and 32:16 has the same phrase for the giant: *na multidão do seu poder*. The image of a multitude of power is the Latin's (πλήθει). *Grandeza* is what a Portuguese ear expects, and the option in 32:16 too. *virtus* → *poder* (row).

*Mentíri* + dative: the enemies will lie to God, i.e. feign submission (MS1932's note: forced homage from the vanquished). 17:46 has the same verb for the same thing: *Os filhos estranhos me mentiram*. The verb stays; explaining it (*vos prestarão falsa homenagem*, MS1932's *homenagens mentirosas*) would be a gloss. Natural order, subject first; the Latin's future kept.

options.label: vos mentirão os vossos inimigos
options.note: the Latin's order; a colon opening on a clitic

options.label: os vossos inimigos vos prestarão falsa homenagem

forms.mentientur: os vossos inimigos vos prestarão falsa homenagem

options.note: MS1932's gloss made the text; explains

decisions.latin: terríbilis in consíliis super fílios hóminum
decisions.why: Verbless, as the Latin: *terríbilis* stands in apposition to *Dei*. *terrível* is singular and so cannot be heard with *as obras*. *consília* are God's purposes over men: *desígnio* (D33), not *conselhos* (advice). No possessive, as the Latin.

options.label: ele é terrível nos seus desígnios

forms.v5b: ele é terrível nos seus desígnios

options.note: copula and possessive supplied (MS1932 *é terrível nos seus desígnios*)

options.label: terrível nos conselhos
options.note: the cognate; D33 keeps it for advice and councils

decisions.latin: Qui convértit … Qui dominátur … Qui pósuit
decisions.why: Three verses open with *Qui*, relative to God named in the verse before, and two of them go on with a clause whose subject is someone else (65:6 *pertransíbunt*, 65:7 *óculi ejus*) — Latin anacoluthon. A Portuguese verse that opens *Que converte* is heard as a question or a wish, and *Ele, que converte o mar em terra seca, pelo rio passarão a pé* does not hold together. So the relative becomes *Ele* + a finite verb (grammar, D2; MS1932 does the same in 65:6–7). The Latin's anaphora survives as *Ele … Ele … Ele*. 32:15, where the verse is two relatives and nothing else, kept *Ele, que*; that build is the option here.

options.label: Ele, que
options.note: the relative kept, as 32:15; the anacoluthon of 65:6–7 then stands in Portuguese

decisions.why: *convértit* is present or perfect by form. The Greek is a present participle (ὁ μεταστρέφων) and DRB has 'turneth'; the verse goes on in the future (*pertransíbunt*, *lætábimur*), which a timeless present carries and a past would jar with. MS1932 makes all three past (*converteu … passaram … alegrámos*), against the Latin's futures. *convértere in* = change into → *converter em* (the row's proposal names 65:6).

*árida* is the dry land (ξηράν; DRB 'dry land'). *Terra seca* says it plainly; MS1932's *terra firme* says what the ground is for, not what it is. 94:5 *áridam fundavérunt manus ejus* will meet the word again.

The formula row *Óculi ejus in páuperem respíciunt* (9:30a = 10:5b) is *Os seus olhos estão voltados para o pobre*, and the row notes 65:7 as near. Kinship kept: *estão voltados para as nações*. The cost is *super* (upon), which *para* flattens; *olham sobre* keeps it but is not said in Portuguese. *Estão postos sobre* keeps it in an idiom (*ter os olhos postos em*).

*Exasperáre* is παραπικραίνω (to embitter, provoke), a different Greek verb from *irritáre* / *exacerbáre* (παροξύνω), which D27 made *provocar*. By D15's test a second Latin–Greek pair keeps its own word, and the cognate *exasperar* exists and is current (to exasperate someone). A blind reader once did not know *exasperou* (9:25, where it was tried for *exacerbáre*) — the risk is known; this reading will test it again. The Latin has no object; *o* (him, God) is supplied because *os que exasperam* is not Portuguese (DRB supplies 'him' too). 67:7 has *qui exásperant* again and 77:8 *exásperans*: a glossary row is proposed.

options.label: os que o exasperam
options.note: draft — the cognate; own Greek verb

options.label: os que o provocam
options.note: DRB 'provoke him'; merges with irritáre / exacerbáre (D27)

options.label: os que o amarguram
options.note: the Greek's image (πικρ-, bitter); in Brazil heard as 'grieve him'

options.label: os rebeldes
options.note: the Hebrew's word (sorerim); not the Latin

decisions.why: Spoken, *Bendizei, nações* is heard first as 'bless the nations' before *o nosso Deus* comes; the glossary's rule for a vocative plural that can be heard as an object is *ó* + noun (28:1). The line is also a versicle alone (*V. Benedícite, gentes, Deum nostrum*, grep).

decisions.latin: Qui pósuit ánimam meam ad vitam
decisions.why: *pónere ad vitam*: set my soul unto life (τοῦ θεμένου τὴν ψυχήν μου εἰς ζωήν; DRB 'set my soul to live'). *pôs a minha alma na vida* keeps the verb and the noun: he placed the soul in life, kept it alive. *para a vida* is closer to *ad* but sounds unfinished; MS1932's *tem conservado a minha vida* paraphrases and turns the soul into 'life'.

options.label: a viver
options.note: DRB 'to live'; the noun becomes a verb

decisions.latin: et non dedit in commotiónem pedes meos
decisions.why: *dare in commotiónem* is σάλος, the Greek of 54:23 *non dabit … fluctuatiónem justo*, which D44 settled as *não deixar vacilar*. One Greek phrase, so one Portuguese (D15's test), and it is what Portuguese says of feet. The word-for-word *não entregou ao abalo* keeps *dare* and the noun but is not said. 120:3 *Non det in commotiónem pedem tuum* should copy.

*indúcere in* is to lead into (εἰσήγαγες). *Induzir* is not possible (it is 'induce, tempt'), *levar* is addúcere's (D42) and *conduzir* collides with the ban on *conduzi*. *Fizestes-nos entrar* is the causative the Greek means; *laço* is the row. MS1932 *Deixaste-nos cair no laço* softens God's act into permission.

options.label: Deixastes-nos cair
options.note: MS1932; permission, not the Latin's act

decisions.why: *Refrigérium* (ἀναψυχή, a cooling, relief) → *refrigério*, the word of 22:2 *aquam refectiónis* and of the Roman Canon's *locum refrigérii*; it keeps the fire-and-water picture of the verse (a cooling after the fire). *edúcere* → *fazer sair* (17:20). MS1932 adds *um lugar de*; *alívio* is plainer but loses the coolness.

decisions.latin: reddam tibi … ófferam tibi … ófferam tibi
decisions.why: Three futures with *tibi*. Mesóclise (*pagar-vos-ei*, *oferecer-vos-ei*) is correct and stands once in 17:50 (*Dar-vos-ei graças*), but three in two verses, two of them five syllables, weigh; Brazilian speech puts the clitic before the verb, and naming the subject *eu* (D2) makes that correct at the head of a colon. *réddere vota → pagar os votos* (row; 21:26, 60:9). The repetition *ófferam tibi … ófferam tibi* is kept word for word.

options.label: eu vos pagarei / Eu vos oferecerei

decisions.why: *distínguere* is to mark off, articulate (διέστειλεν: uttered distinctly). Said of lips it is to pronounce the vow in so many words. *pronunciaram* (MS1932) says it; *distinguiram* would be heard as 'told apart'.

options.label: articularam
options.note: closest to the root sense; clinical

decisions.why: The verse continues the relative of 65:13 (*vota … quæ distinxérunt lábia mea, et [quæ] locútum est os meum*). *E que a minha boca falou* keeps that link, so the vows are what the mouth spoke; *E a minha boca falou* reads as a new sentence and leaves 'what' unsaid. *loqui → falar*.

options.label: E que a minha boca falou

forms.v14: E que a minha boca falou

options.label: e que a minha boca proferiu

forms.v14: E que a minha boca proferiu

decisions.why: *medullátus* is 'full of marrow', hence rich, fat (L&S; μεμυαλωμένα). The concrete image stays (rule 5: bones, fat): *cheios de tutano*, *tutano* being the plain Brazilian word for marrow. MS1932 *pingues* and pt-style *gordos* keep richness but lose the marrow; *gordo* is *pinguis*'s (19:4).

*incénsum* (θυμίαμα) is what goes up in smoke — here from burnt rams. *incenso* is the Latin's word and a Portuguese reader knows it as the altar's smoke; the rams make clear it is not resin. MS1932's *fumo* explains; *fumaça* is fumus's. *aríes → carneiro* (row).

options.label: com incenso de carneiros
options.note: draft — no articles, as the Latin; two syllables fewer on a colon already +3

options.label: com o incenso dos carneiros
options.note: the articles supplied; the colon +5 on the Latin

decisions.why: Bare *ouvi* is also 'I heard' (rule 3; D13 keeps the ban on the bare form, D18 refused an exception for a verse where another imperative has sounded). 48:2 *Audíte hæc* recast the same way: *Escutai* (the audíre row: 'recast or use escutar there and note it'). The cost: *escutar* is exaudíre's (D3), and 65:18–19 has *exaudíre* twice. *Vinde … ouvi* is the option, one touch away; *Vinde, e vede* (65:5) and *Vinde, escutai* (65:16) keep the Latin's pair of calls.

options.label: ouvi
options.note: the row's verb; bare, banned (D1, D13)

decisions.why: *quanta* (neuter plural): how great things / how much (ὅσα). *fecit* has God as its hidden subject, named (*ele*). The dative of advantage *ánimæ meæ* is *pela minha alma* — *fez à minha alma* is heard as something done to the soul, for good or ill. MS1932 *quão grandes coisas ele fez à minha alma* is the fuller wording, three syllables longer.

options.label: quanto ele fez pela minha alma

forms.quanta: quanto ele fez pela minha alma

options.label: quão grandes coisas ele fez pela minha alma

forms.quanta: quão grandes coisas ele fez pela minha alma

options.label: quanto ele fez à minha alma

forms.quanta: quanto ele fez à minha alma

decisions.why: *exaltávi* has no object in the Latin or the Greek (ὕψωσα); the object is plainly God, named at the head of the verse (*Ad ipsum*). Portuguese *exaltar* cannot stand absolute, so *o* is supplied (grammar; DRB and MS1932 supply 'him' too). *sub lingua mea* is the Latin's image — 'under my tongue', the praise held ready in the mouth — and stays; DRB and MS1932 flatten it to 'with my tongue'.

options.label: e exaltei
options.note: absolute, as the Latin; not Portuguese

decisions.latin: Iniquitátem si aspéxi in corde meo
decisions.why: The Latin is a real condition: perfect indicative, then future (*non exáudiet*). MS1932 turns it counterfactual (*Se eu tivesse visto … não me ouviria*), which states that he did not; the Latin leaves it to 65:19 to say so. Mood is grammar (D2), but here the indicative carries the logic of the next verse, so it is kept. *aspícere* → *contemplar* (to look at and dwell on; DRB 'looked at'): *ver* is vidére's and *olhar* is respícere's in 32:13. The subject *eu* is named because the verse opens on the condition.

options.label: Se eu olhei para a iniquidade

forms.aspexi: Se eu olhei para a iniquidade

options.label: Se eu tivesse visto a iniquidade

forms.aspexi: Se eu tivesse visto a iniquidade

options.note: MS1932's counterfactual (it would want *escutaria* in the second colon)

decisions.latin: non exáudiet Dóminus … Proptérea exaudívit Deus
decisions.why: Both hearings have no object in the Latin (the Greek adds μου in 65:19). *escutar* can stand absolute in Portuguese, so none is added; MS1932 adds *me* twice. *exaudíre → escutar* (D3).

*Benedíctus Dóminus* is verbless in the finished psalms (*Bendito o Senhor*, 27:6, 30:22, 40:14): the article makes it a predication. *Deus* takes no article, and *Bendito Deus, que …* is heard first as a vocative ('blessed God, who …') in a verse that goes on in the third person. The copula *seja* (D2) removes that; it is also MS1932's wording. 67:36 ends on the same two words.

options.label: Bendito Deus
options.note: verbless as the Latin and as 27:6

choices.65:1: The psalm starts at 65:1 with the titulus dropped (D7; DO's 65:1 has *Jubiláte* already). *jubiláre → aclamar* (D43; the row names 65:1). *omnis terra* as vocative: *toda a terra*. 65:1 is the Introit of the third Sunday after Easter and an Offertory (Epi2-0), grep.
choices.65:3: *Dícite Deo: Quam …* — the quoted speech turns to God (*vós*) while the frame speaks of him. *Quam terribília* → *Como são terríveis* (8:2a *como é admirável*); *terríbilis → terrível* (D43; the row names 65:3). The second colon is lowercase after the *!*, as the Latin.
choices.65:4: *Omnis terra adóret te* — the subjunctive of wish (*adore*, *entoe*). Each colon reads alone (the Epiphany versicle). Both cola +3 on the Latin: the D25 cost (*entoar salmos* for *psállere*); accepted.
choices.65:5: *Veníte, et vidéte ópera* — *Vinde, e vede as obras* word for word 45:9 (*ópera Dómini* there, *Dei* here).
choices.65:6: *in flúmine pertransíbunt pede* → *pelo rio passarão a pé* (*in* of passage; MS1932 *pelo rio*). The Latin's futures kept, the subject 'they' left unnamed as the Latin leaves it. *ibi lætábimur in ipso* → *ali nos alegraremos nele*.
choices.65:7: *in virtúte sua* → *com o seu poder* (instrumental here; 20:2 *no vosso poder* is where the king rejoices). *in ætérnum → para sempre* (D23). *non exalténtur in semetípsis* → *não se exaltem em si mesmos* (the jussive; *exaltar* row).
choices.65:8: *audítam fácite vocem* → *fazei ouvir a voz* (the *vocem dare* row, 17:14 *fez ouvir a sua voz*). The Latin ends the verse on a comma, carried into 65:9; so does the Portuguese.
choices.65:10: Two verbs kept two, as the *examináre / probáre* row asks for this very verse: *provastes … examinastes … se examina*; *no fogo* as 16:3, 11:7, 17:31.
choices.65:11: *in dorso nostro* → *nas nossas costas* (17:41 *dar as costas*; *dorso* is an animal's). *posuísti … imposuísti* → *pusestes … pusestes* (*impónere super → pôr sobre*, D44): the Latin's two verbs share their root, so the near-repetition is the Latin's; the Greek has two verbs (ἔθου, ἐπεβίβασας 'made to ride').
choices.65:12: *per ignem et aquam* → *pelo fogo e pela água* (the preposition repeated, as Portuguese needs).
choices.65:13: *in holocáustis* → *com holocaustos* (DRB, MS1932). *holocáustum → holocausto* (row, which names 65:13, 65:15).
choices.65:15: *boves cum hircis* → *bois com bodes* (the *hircus* row asks 65:15 to copy 49:9, 13). The Latin's object-first order is not kept in the first colon: the verb first is natural, and the two colons then open alike, as they do in meaning. The first colon is still +3 on the Latin (the future *oferecerei* and *cheios de tutano* for two Latin words); accepted — the marrow is the Latin's image.
choices.65:16: *omnes, qui timétis Deum* → *todos vós que temeis a Deus* (21:24 *Vós que temeis o Senhor*); *e eu narrarei* names the speaker as the call turns to his own story. The Offertory (Pasc3/Epi) uses 65:16 with *narrábo vobis* and *fecit Dóminus*; the psalm has neither. The second colon +3: *ele* names the subject so that *fez* is not heard as the speaker's; kept.
choices.65:17: *Ad ipsum ore meo clamávi* → *A ele clamei com a minha boca* — the Latin's order kept at the head (*A ele*), the colon ending on *boca*, which answers *língua* at the end of the verse, as *ore … lingua* do.
choices.65:19: *Proptérea → Por isso* (17:50). *atténdit voci deprecatiónis meæ* → *atendeu à voz da minha prece* (D3 *atender*; D35 *prece*; 27:6).
choices.65:20: *amovére → afastar* (row). *et misericórdiam suam a me* → *nem a sua misericórdia de mim*: *et* under a negation is *nem* (grammar); *a me* at the end, where the Latin has it, so that it governs both nouns as in the Latin.

audit.note: Psalm-level draft from consult/parallels/ps065.md (no DM1962: Ps 65 is not a psalm of the day hours). Hard readings: 65:6–7 the relative *Qui* with anacoluthon (decision `qui`); 65:6 *convértit* present or past (the Greek's participle decides); 65:7 *qui exásperant* (a second Greek verb beside D27's *provocar*); 65:9 *ad vitam*; 65:13–14 the relative carried across two prayed verses; 65:15 *medulláta*, *incénsum aríetum*; 65:16 *audíte* under the *ouvi* ban; 65:18 the real condition. Glossary applied: aclamar (D43), entoar salmos / entoar um salmo (D25), terrível (D43), desígnio (D33), converter em (row proposal), para sempre (D23), provar / examinar (row), laço, pôr sobre (D44), refrigério (22:2), pagar os votos, holocausto, carneiro, bode (D44), escutar / atender / prece (D3, D35), não deixar vacilar (D44, σάλος), afastar. Liturgical uses by grep: 65:1–2 Introit Pasc3-0 and Offertory Epi2-0; 65:4 the Epiphany versicle and a Matins antiphon; 65:8–9, 20 Offertory Pasc5-0 (with *Dóminum* and other variants); 65:16 Offertories (with *vobis*, *Dóminus* added); *V. Benedícite, gentes, Deum nostrum*.

Hard checks pass. Soft length flags accepted: 65:4 both cola +3 (D25's *entoar salmos*), 65:15a +3 (*cheios de tutano*; articles dropped to bring it from +5), 65:16b +3 (*ele* named); 65:3, 65:9b, 65:11a, 65:19 are 3–4 syllables short, which the tone absorbs. No rhyme flags. Oxytone cadences are within the rule (last or second-last syllable).
